title: York police chief says 17-year-old shot dead in Aurora highlights dangers officers face
subtitle: Mikail Rashid was shot dead after officers responded to a call about a break and enter on Downey Circle, near Bayview Avenue and St. John's Side Road, around 7:45 p.m. on Wednesday, according to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which probes deaths involving police.
article: The York Regional police chief says the "exchange of gunfire" between police and the 17-year-old boy who was killed in the shootout in Aurora earlier this week is a tragic event and an example of the challenges officers face daily.

Days after Mikail Rashid was shot dead, York police chief Jim MacSween released a statement saying the fatal shooting involving police "brings to the forefront the increasing levels of violence experienced by our front-line members while they work diligently to maintain order and public safety."

Rashid was shot dead after officers responded to a call about a break and enter on Downey Circle, near Bayview Avenue and St. John's Side Road, around 7:45 p.m. on Wednesday, according to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which probes deaths involving police.
Soon after, there was "an exchange of gunfire" between a 17-year-old and police officers along a stretch of Downey Circle. The teen was struck multiple times and pronounced dead at the scene.
One officer was taken to hospital with minor injuries, the SIU said.
The agency is investigating the circumstances of the shooting, including who called 911 and what led to the gunfire.

In an interview with the Star on Thursday, Rashid's mother, Lala Rukh, said Rashid lived at a home on Downey Circle with her ex-husband, just steps away from where she and neighbours recalled seeing his body.
She said Rashid was home alone eating dinner - his father had just left to go to the gym - before the gunfire broke out.
"I don't know what happened," Rukh said, struggling to understand how her son ended up dead following a report about a break-and-enter.
"It does not make sense. He would not break and enter into his own house. Why would he need to? He has the keys."

An SIU spokesperson declined to comment on what weapon the teen had used in the exchange of gunfire with police, saying the agency cannot release those details at this point in the investigation. Rukh doesn't know herself, but said Rashid's father owned a shotgun and Rashid had an antique sword and knife collection.
At the scene on Thursday, neighbours shared with the Star photographs that show the ground littered with evidence markers, including those marking what appeared to be a shotgun and a black machete.

Multiple residents along the tree-lined street reported hearing several gunshots on the Wednesday evening - what some initially thought were fireworks. By Thursday morning, media and spectators swarmed the police tape that cordoned off a large stretch of Downey Circle, including Rashid's home where an officer could be seen stationed in the backyard, next to a broken screen door.
Neighbours next to the house said their home was damaged by the gunfire, with several bullet holes in their garage and front door.
MacSween, in his statement, called the fatal shooting a "tragic event" and "one more example of the challenges our officers face each and every day."

Pointing to the general increase in violent crime in York Region this year, MacSween said he's heard from residents on a daily basis who are feeling "increasingly vulnerable" to becoming a victim of crime.
"This is concerning to me and simply unacceptable."
MacSween said that while officers are working tirelessly to ensure the safety and well-being of the community, the environment they're working in has "become increasingly dangerous."

According to York police, there have been 952 incidents in the last five years in which officers were the victim of an assault. So far this year, 116 officers have been attacked and assaulted in incidents, 13 of which involved a weapon.

A Grade 12 student at Dr. G.W. Williams Secondary School in Aurora, Rashid is being remembered by friends and family as a bright, smart and loving kid who enjoyed playing video games, baking and sciences.
Rashid was studying hard to get his grades up and apply to medical schools - he wanted to join the humanitarian charity Doctors Without Borders, said his mom, Rukh.
In a statement from the York Regional District School Board, officials said their thoughts are with those involved and affected by the incident.

"As a school board, our focus today and in the days ahead is to provide support to those who attend our schools in this area," the spokesperson said, noting the board's mental health clinicians will be on-site and available to students who need support.
Rukh said she is working on finalizing the details for Rashid's funeral. It was only two years ago that she had to bury her father.
"I didn't think I'd have to do it again this soon," she said tearfully. "My dad was my rock, and my son was my rock. I don't have any rocks anymore."
